elements.element: Customer may assign to an affiliate without consent.
elements.evidence: Revised 20(d) permits assignment only "to a successor to its business upon written notice"; any other assignment (including to an affiliate) "requires the other party's written consent." No affiliate carve-out was inserted.

elements.element: Customer may assign to a successor in a merger, acquisition, or sale of substantially all assets without consent.
elements.evidence: "Either party may assign this Agreement to a successor to its business upon written notice to the other party" — notice only, no consent. (Wording is generic "successor to its business" rather than the enumerated merger/acquisition/asset-sale triggers, but it operates without consent.)

elements.element: Vendor may not assign without Customer's consent.
elements.evidence: The successor right is mutual ("Either party"), so Vendor may assign to a successor to its business on notice alone; the preferred position requires Customer consent for any Vendor assignment. Deleting "not assign this Agreement or" from Section 3(c) also removed the standing bar on Sparkling assigning without Garman's written authorization.

elements.element: Customer's consent to Vendor assignment is not to be unreasonably withheld.
elements.evidence: "any other assignment requires the other party's written consent, which shall not be unreasonably withheld" — applies symmetrically, so Customer's consent to a non-successor Vendor assignment is on a reasonableness standard.

elements.element: Vendor may never assign to a Customer competitor.
elements.evidence: No competitor prohibition appears in revised 20(d) or elsewhere in the rendered language; a Vendor successor assignment on notice could be to a Customer competitor.

elements.element: Customer's change of control gives Vendor no termination right.
elements.evidence: Condition does not apply: the cited provisions and the finding record contain no change-of-control clause, deemed-assignment trigger, or Vendor termination/re-pricing right on Customer's change of control, and the redline introduces none.

elements.element: Both parties may assign to a successor.
elements.evidence: "Either party may assign this Agreement to a successor to its business" — expressly mutual.

elements.element: A successor assignment requires written notice.
elements.evidence: "...to a successor to its business upon written notice to the other party."

"any other assignment requires the other party's written consent"; no residual no-consent exception survives — the only remaining Section 3(c) restrictions concern transfer, lease, export or sublicence of the Work, not assignment of the Agreement.

elements.element: Consent to other assignments is not to be unreasonably withheld.
elements.evidence: "...written consent, which shall not be unreasonably withheld."

reasons: Fallback checklist is complete on the operative text of revised Section 20(d): mutual successor assignment on written notice, consent for other assignments, reasonableness standard. The finding is correctly targeted at the fallback and the original flat mutual bar was indeed walk-away territory (no M&A carve-out for Customer).

Preferred level is incomplete: no affiliate carve-out for Customer, no absolute Customer-consent gate on Vendor assignment (the mutual successor right lets Vendor assign on notice alone), and no bar on assignment to a Customer competitor. To reach preferred the drafter would need to split the clause — e.g. "Customer may assign to an affiliate or to a successor in a merger, acquisition or sale of substantially all assets without consent; Vendor may not assign without Customer's prior written consent, not to be unreasonably withheld, and in no event to a competitor of Customer."

Minimality holds. The Section 3(c) edit is a narrow conforming deletion of only "assign this Agreement or" — necessary because a retained absolute bar on Sparkling assigning without Garman's written authorization would directly contradict the new mutual successor right in 20(d). The rest of 3(c) (transfer, lease, export, sublicence of the Work) is preserved intact, and no survival tails, procedures, or extra requirements were added.

Intent is preserved: no undefined terms, no dangling cross-references, and the Work-transfer controls in 3(c), which serve a different purpose from assignment of the Agreement, survive unchanged. No change-of-control mechanic exists to disturb.

Note for the record: the conforming 3(c) deletion does relax a Customer-favourable restriction on Vendor's assignment rights. If the team wants to keep that protection, the cleaner fix at preferred level is to restore "not assign this Agreement" in 3(c) and make the 20(d) successor right Customer-only.
